headline: AI agents get their own cloud computers, sparking a new economy with massive infrastructure costs
summary: OpenAI's Dots, an agent with its own cloud computer, browser, and apps, highlights a shift where AI incurs significant infrastructure costs. Anthropic's $518 billion commitment over a decade underscores this new economic reality.
details: OpenAI's Dots, unveiled at DevDay 2026, is an AI agent with its own cloud computer, browser, and connected apps, capable of continuous work even when your laptop is off. This raises questions about who pays for these always-on AI resources.

Dots operates on its own cloud machine, allowing users to monitor its progress at any time. It integrates with ChatGPT across desktop, web, and mobile, and also communicates via Slack and Teams, with SMS messaging planned.

The agent is designed for proactive research, identifying helpful tasks using only connected read-only apps when not actively engaged. This mechanism ensures security by preventing it from sending messages, editing content, or controlling your computer.

Security features include using saved passwords for web logins without exposing them to the model, and keeping the agent's computer separate from the user's unless explicitly linked. This design aims to build user trust.

The shift means agent owners pay not just for the model, but also for the underlying compute infrastructure. Anthropic's IPO documents reveal a staggering $518 billion commitment over the next decade for compute and hosting with partners like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft.

Approximately 80% of Anthropic's $518 billion commitment is non-cancellable, meaning costs are incurred regardless of actual usage. This includes $111.1 billion with Google, $110 billion with Amazon, and $31.4 billion with Microsoft, plus $161.2 billion for Broadcom equipment leases.

These long-term contracts, spanning up to a decade, highlight a major shift in the AI industry's economic model. Companies are securing vast amounts of specialized processing power, driven by supply constraints rather than demand.

Anthropic explains to investors that access to compute power is becoming the primary bottleneck for AI development, anticipating future demand for advanced AI systems will outstrip production capacity. This creates complex relationships where partners are also investors, customers, and competitors.

headline: ISO 42001 vs EU AI Act: Not interchangeable, but both can strengthen AI governance
summary: While both address AI risk management, ISO 42001 is an international standard for an AI Management System, whereas the EU AI Act is binding legislation with specific legal requirements for AI systems.
details: As organizations increasingly adopt artificial intelligence, AI governance is becoming a critical business requirement. Discussions often revolve around two key frameworks: ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act.
At first glance, these frameworks may appear to tackle the same issues, involving AI risk management, governance, documentation, and oversight. However, they are designed for distinct purposes.

ISO 42001 provides a management-system framework, guiding organizations to establish a structured approach for managing AI-related risks responsibly across their operations. It helps create repeatable processes as an AI portfolio grows.

The EU AI Act, conversely, is binding European legislation. It employs a risk-based approach to establish legal obligations for various AI systems and actors, including providers and deployers operating within the European market.
For many companies, utilizing both frameworks can provide a more robust governance structure. However, ISO 42001 certification does not automatically fulfill an organization's EU AI Act obligations.

The EU AI Act specifically defines stringent requirements for high-risk AI systems. These include detailed mandates for risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, and post-market monitoring throughout the system's lifecycle.

Implementing an AI management system under ISO 42001 is not the same as demonstrating compliance with a specific law. An organization might have mature AI governance processes but still needs to assess if individual AI systems fall under the EU AI Act's high-risk categories.

Organizations should avoid treating one framework as a substitute for the other. Instead, it is more effective to understand where their approaches overlap and where they remain distinct, leveraging both for comprehensive AI governance.
